title: Speaking, asking: pi'el
topic: the pi'el binyan in the present and the past
why: You discover the idea of the binyan, the mold a root is poured into to make a verb, with a second, very common mold: pi'el (to speak, to ask for, to look for), in the present and the past. It's the key that will open up hitpa'el and hif'il in the next unit.

{"lessons": ["

The binyan: a mold for verbs

In Hebrew, a verb is a root (usually three consonants, which carry the meaning) poured into a mold (which supplies the vowels, the prefixes, and the type of action). This mold is called a binyan (בִּנְיָן, \"construction\"). There are seven of them.

So far, you've used the first one, pa'al: כּוֹתֵב, כָּתַב, יִכְתֹּב. Today, the second one: pi'el. The same root can go into two molds, with two related meanings:

לוֹמֵד / מְלַמֵּדhe learns (pa'al) / he teaches (pi'el) [lomed / melamed]

English uses two unrelated words, \"learn\" and \"teach\"; Hebrew keeps the same root and simply switches molds.

You already know the root ב־ק־שׁ (to ask for): it's in בְּבַקָּשָׁה, \"please.\"

", "

Pi'el in the present

Three signs help you recognize it: a מְ at the beginning, the vowels a then e, and a dot (dagesh) in the middle letter. Like every present tense, it has four forms:

Formto speakto ask forto look for
m. sg.מְדַבֵּר medaberמְבַקֵּשׁ mevakeshמְחַפֵּשׂ mekhapes
f. sg.מְדַבֶּרֶת medaberetמְבַקֶּשֶׁת mevakeshetמְחַפֶּשֶׂת mekhapeset
m. pl.מְדַבְּרִים medabrimמְבַקְּשִׁים mevakshimמְחַפְּשִׂים mekhapsim
f. pl.מְדַבְּרוֹת medabrotמְבַקְּשׁוֹת mevakshotמְחַפְּשׂוֹת mekhapsot

The infinitive is in לְ־: לְדַבֵּר (ledaber), לְבַקֵּשׁ (levakesh), לְחַפֵּשׂ (lekhapes). Other verbs in the same mold: מְשַׁלֵּם (to pay), מְבַקֵּר (to visit), מְסַפֵּר (to tell a story), מְלַמֵּד (to teach).

The trap: English \"ask\" has two Hebrew translations. מְבַקֵּשׁ is asking for something (הוּא מְבַקֵּשׁ כּוֹס מַיִם); to ask a question, you say שׁוֹאֵל (pa'al).

", "

Pi'el in the past

In the past, pi'el starts with an i: דִּבֵּר (he spoke). The endings are exactly the past-tense endings you know (־תִּי, ־תָּ, ־נוּ…).

Pronounto speakto ask forto look for
אֲנִידִּבַּרְתִּי dibartiבִּקַּשְׁתִּי bikashtiחִפַּשְׂתִּי khipasti
אַתָּהדִּבַּרְתָּ dibartaבִּקַּשְׁתָּ bikashtaחִפַּשְׂתָּ khipasta
אַתְּדִּבַּרְתְּ dibartבִּקַּשְׁתְּ bikashtחִפַּשְׂתְּ khipast
הוּאדִּבֵּר diberבִּקֵּשׁ bikeshחִפֵּשׂ khipes
הִיאדִּבְּרָה dibraבִּקְּשָׁה bikshaחִפְּשָׂה khipsa
אֲנַחְנוּדִּבַּרְנוּ dibarnuבִּקַּשְׁנוּ bikashnuחִפַּשְׂנוּ khipasnu
אַתֶּםדִּבַּרְתֶּם dibartemבִּקַּשְׁתֶּם bikashtemחִפַּשְׂתֶּם khipastem
אַתֶּןדִּבַּרְתֶּן dibartenבִּקַּשְׁתֶּן bikashtenחִפַּשְׂתֶּן khipasten
הֵם / הֵןדִּבְּרוּ dibruבִּקְּשׁוּ bikshuחִפְּשׂוּ khipsu

Listen carefully to the first letter: מְבַקֵּשׁ is read mevakesh (v), but בִּקֵּשׁ is read bikesh (b), because the ב has a dot at the start of a word. It's the dagesh you saw with the alef-bet.

אֶתְמוֹל דִּבַּרְתִּי עִם בַּעַל הַדִּירָה.Yesterday, I spoke with the landlord. [etmol dibarti im ba'al ha-dira]
הִיא חִפְּשָׂה דִּירָה בְּחֵיפָה.She looked for an apartment in Haifa. [hi khipsa dira be-Kheifa]
